carolina.name: Carolina Vasconcelos
carolina.headline: Bridges product direction, complex UX and engineering execution.
carolina.intro: Carolina is a product-minded UX/UI and technical profile with experience across product ownership, complex B2B SaaS, operational products and frontend delivery.
paragraphs: Her strongest contribution is turning ambiguous business priorities and user needs into focused scope, understandable journeys and buildable product increments. She can move from discovery and roadmap structure into information architecture, interaction models, user stories, acceptance criteria and release preparation without losing the reason the product is being built.

Because she has led UX/UI and frontend modernisation in constraint-heavy environments, she designs with system states, edge cases, component logic, accessibility and implementation realities in view. This makes her especially valuable in products where dashboards, datasets, maps, filters, alerts and operational workflows must become clear without oversimplifying the system.

values.title: Product direction
values.copy: Clarifies the problem, defines focused scope and connects roadmap priorities with user and business value.

values.title: Complex experience design
values.copy: Structures data-heavy and operational workflows into coherent journeys, states and reusable interaction patterns.

values.title: Design-to-delivery bridge
values.copy: Carries decisions into Figma, component logic, acceptance criteria, frontend plans, QA and release preparation.

evidence.title: Product Manager / Product Design Owner · Nommon
evidence.copy: Owns discovery, roadmap structure, backlog quality and UX direction for a multi-product SaaS platform in mobility and data intelligence.

evidence.title: Senior Frontend Developer & UX/UI Lead · Siemens Mobility
evidence.copy: Led the UX/UI and frontend modernisation of a legacy operational product, balancing usability with architecture, integrations and delivery risk.

evidence.title: UX Advisor · PsyPilot
evidence.copy: Supports early product decisions, service flows and information architecture for psychologists, clinic teams and patients.

carmelo.name: Carmelo Alcaraz Coy
carmelo.headline: Turns product requirements into reliable systems and technical foundations.
carmelo.intro: Carmelo is a software and platform engineer with a dual academic background in Computer Engineering and Mathematics, and a career spanning development, architecture, cloud and infrastructure.
paragraphs: His progression from software engineer to senior software engineer and platform engineer gives him a broad view of how applications are designed, operated and evolved. He can connect backend services, APIs, databases and web applications with the cloud and automation capabilities that development teams need to deliver consistently.

His mathematical foundation adds structured analytical thinking to architecture and engineering decisions. He is particularly useful where a product needs more than implementation: explicit technical trade-offs, maintainable system design, infrastructure as code, platform capabilities and a foundation that can support long-term change.

values.title: System architecture
values.copy: Designs software structures, services, APIs and data foundations around product needs and technical constraints.

values.title: Cloud & platform engineering
values.copy: Connects AWS, Azure, Docker and cloud operations with the capabilities teams need to build and run software.

values.title: Automation & reliability
values.copy: Uses Terraform, Ansible and Infrastructure as Code to reduce manual work and create repeatable technical foundations.

evidence.title: Platform Engineer · Nommon
evidence.copy: Designs and operates cloud-based platforms, infrastructure automation and internal engineering solutions that support software teams.

evidence.title: Senior Software Engineer · Nommon
evidence.copy: Worked across software architecture, system design, web applications, data visualisation and technical leadership within project teams.

evidence.title: Software Engineer · Capgemini
evidence.copy: Built and maintained enterprise software using established engineering methodologies, with experience in Java and C/C++.

evidence.title: Computer Engineering + Mathematics
evidence.copy: Combines software engineering with optimisation, statistics, numerical methods, modelling and analytical problem solving.

translations.allOne: Content + styles + behaviour in one file
translations.briefQuote: “We had two complementary senior profiles, but no clear way to package, explain and sell their combined value.”
translations.briefTitle: Two strong profiles did not automatically create one strong proposition.
translations.categoryDecision: Use a recognised category: Product & Engineering Studio.
translations.categoryDecisionNote: Let the differentiation come from the problems we solve, our shared working context and the way product and technology stay connected.
translations.ctaCopy: Let’s discuss how to turn it into a focused product direction and a technical foundation your team can build on.
translations.ctaTitle: Have a complex problem that still feels difficult to frame?
translations.distinctiveOutcome: We kept the principle — product thinking and builder mindset — but replaced the invented category.
translations.distinctiveQuote: Distinctive was not the same as clear.
translations.f6: Senior support for critical product initiatives
translations.faviconCopy: The mark was tested from a social/app presentation down to the 16px browser context, in light and dark modes.
translations.focusIntro: We started with a better question: where does our combination create an advantage that a client can recognise?
translations.focusTitle: We did not start with “What skills do we have?”
translations.friction1: It did not clearly say that we design and build software.
translations.friction2: It could sound like AI, education or product coaching.
translations.friction3: It required explanation before trust could start.
translations.heroLede: The website was only the visible output. The real work was turning two complementary senior profiles into a proposition the market could understand, trust and hire.
translations.initialRequest: What we initially thought we needed
translations.initialRequestNote: A place to show two profiles, list skills and provide contact details.
translations.mBuildNote: Design, code and structure support the same decision.
translations.mChooseNote: Keep the useful principle, remove the confusing implementation.
translations.mEvolveNote: Add modularity and integrations when the product earns them.
translations.mFrameNote: Do not confuse the requested output with the underlying need.
translations.mResearchNote: Understand how buyers already describe the category.
translations.mShapeNote: Validate the proposition before expanding the system.
translations.marketIntro: The goal was not to copy another studio. It was to identify the category signals that reduce explanation and the gaps where our own positioning needed to be specific.
translations.marketTitle: We looked for language buyers already understood.
translations.modularReason: Structure, presentation, behaviour and assets can now evolve independently.
translations.mvpIntro: The first version was deliberately monolithic. It made content and positioning cheap to change. Modularity arrived only when languages, themes, profile dialogs, visual assets and new pages created real maintenance pressure.
translations.mvpQuote: MVP means delaying complexity — not avoiding good foundations forever.
translations.mvpReason: Right for rapid iteration while the proposition was still changing.
translations.mvpTitle: We validated the proposition before optimising the architecture.
translations.nameLede: The idea captured our mindset, but it asked the buyer to decode the category before understanding the offer.
translations.nephelixLearning: The model explains embedded support well, but works better for us as a collaboration format than as a lead service.
translations.nephelixSignal: Signal: direct senior access, fewer agency layers and less context loss between product and implementation.
translations.p1c: The requested output is not always the real problem.
translations.p2c: Market language helps separate novelty from useful differentiation.
translations.p3c: A buyer should understand the value before interpreting the brand.
translations.p4c: Experience, architecture and delivery shape each other.
translations.p5c: Validate the proposition before paying for optional complexity.
translations.p6c: The foundation grows when real maintenance and product needs justify it.
translations.problemSpaces: Problem spaces where both perspectives matter
translations.realProblemNote: The challenge was differentiation: making years of shared context, complementary depth and 360° product thinking visible without exposing confidential client work.
translations.realProblemValue: A credible reason to hire us as one product and engineering unit.
translations.repoCopy: The repository now supports multiple pages and separate assets without introducing a framework or deployment complexity the project does not need.
translations.repoTitle: The architecture changed when the product earned it.
translations.sharedCopy: Positioning, services, content architecture, prioritisation and the repository structure were joint decisions. Carolina led branding, UX/UI and frontend execution; Carmelo focused on technical review, performance, accessibility and the next integration foundations.
translations.sharedTitle: Every important decision could be challenged from both product and technical perspectives.
translations.showsIntro: Client work involves deeper systems and constraints, but the same reasoning remains visible here.
translations.showsTitle: The website is the example. The decisions are the product.
translations.thoughtbotLearning: Breadth is credible when it is organised around product stages and client needs.
translations.thoughtbotSignal: Signal: product strategy, design, development, platform work and team enablement across the lifecycle.
translations.ustwoLearning: Recognisable and credible, but the category can still feel design-led.
translations.ustwoSignal: Signal: human-centred design and technical expertise presented as one full-stack product capability.
translations.v1Copy: Fast to build and useful for testing content, but long, dark and still close to a list of services.
translations.v2Copy: The first screen explained more, profiles became visible earlier and the layout used familiar component patterns.
translations.v3Copy: The system moved to a proprietary blue–purple language, stronger contrast, accessible states and a more focused proposition.
translations.visualIntro: Familiar interaction patterns reduced effort. A proprietary blue–purple identity, related portraits and consistent light/dark states made the two profiles feel intentionally connected.
translations.visualTitle: The visual system had to make the same argument as the copy.
translations.vp6b: Reusable design and modular technical systems
translations.vr1: Blue and purple connect product and engineering without assigning rigid silos.
translations.vr2: Large statements explain the value before detailed components compete for attention.
translations.vr3: Photos feel individual but intentionally related.
translations.vr4: English, Spanish and Portuguese are not decorative localisation — they are languages we work in.
translations.vr5: Light, dark, responsive and keyboard states are part of the product, not finishing touches.
translations.whatNotSell: What we chose not to sell as our main proposition
translations.workcoLearning: Premium positioning comes from clarity and proof, not decorative complexity.
translations.workcoSignal: Signal: outcome-first language focused on solving complex problems rather than describing a long service list.
translations.worked1: It expressed product thinking rather than simple execution.
translations.worked2: It reflected a builder mindset and joint ownership.
translations.worked3: It was memorable and gave the studio personality.
translations.workedExample: A worked example of how we think
translations.deferredTitle: A focused phase also needs an explicit “not now.”
translations.deferredIntro: We separated what was necessary to validate the proposition and start conversations from what would only make the studio look more finished. These items were deferred, not forgotten.
translations.deferredBrandCopy: We kept Carolina & Carmelo and a recognised category while the proposition was still being tested. A permanent name should follow clarity, not replace it.
translations.deferredDomainCopy: GitHub Pages was enough to publish and learn. A domain and branded inbox become valuable once the final name is worth committing to.
translations.deferredRolloutCopy: The current mark, palette and interface system create coherence. A full identity manual, templates and broader launch assets would add polish, but not validate the offer.
translations.deferredProofCopy: We did not manufacture portfolio evidence from confidential company work. More public cases will be added when there is permission or new work that can be shown properly.
translations.deferredRule: Defer anything that does not change the next customer decision.
